title: Technical Interview Preparation
description: Prepare for coding and system design interviews with core data structures, repeatable problem-solving strategies, system design fundamentals, and the communication skills interviewers actually score.
objectives: Analyze time and space complexity and pick the right data structure
Break an unfamiliar problem into a working approach before coding
Design a scalable service and defend the trade-offs you make
Communicate clearly under pressure using structured answers
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with arrays, maps, and functions
Comfort writing and running small programs

modules.title: Data Structures & Algorithms Fundamentals
modules.description: Complexity analysis and the core structures that show up in nearly every coding interview.
modules.completionCriteria: Analyze a function's time and space complexity and choose the right structure for a lookup-heavy problem without hints.

lessons.title: Big-O and Complexity Analysis
objectives: Classify common algorithms by growth rate
Estimate the time and space cost of a loop-heavy function

content.introduction: Interviewers care less about memorized line counts and more about how your solution's cost grows as the input grows. Big-O is the language you use to say that out loud before you write code.
content.explanation: Big-O describes how time or memory scales with input size n, dropping constants and lower-order terms: one pass over an array is O(n), two nested loops are O(n^2), halving the search range each step is O(log n), and sorting is typically O(n log n). When analyzing, count the dominant operation — comparisons, lookups, hash operations — and separate average from worst case, because a hash map is O(1) on average but degrades toward O(n) under heavy collisions. Always report space too: an array you build is O(n), and a recursive depth-first search can hold O(n) frames on the call stack.

examples.title: An O(n) solution using a hash set
examples.walkthrough: Each element is checked against the set once, so the loop dominates at O(n). The set stores at most n elements, giving O(n) extra space — far better than the O(n^2) pair-checking version.

content.useCase: Justifying your approach before coding: 'this is O(n) time and O(n) space because of the set' tells the interviewer you understand the cost of your design.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the average-case time complexity of a hash set lookup?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Hashing computes an index directly, so lookups are constant time on average (worst case O(n) with pathological collisions).

knowledgeCheck.question: A loop over n items that runs a second full loop over the same n items each iteration is:
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The inner loop runs about n times for each of the n outer iterations, giving n × n = O(n^2).

content.summary: Big-O measures growth, not absolute speed. Count the dominant operation, report average and worst case, and always include space.

lessons.title: Arrays, Hash Maps, and Strings
objectives: Choose between an array, map, and set
Solve frequency and membership problems efficiently

content.introduction: Most interview problems hinge on one decision: which structure makes the check I need fast? Arrays win at ordered indexed access; hash maps and sets win at lookup by value.
content.explanation: Arrays give O(1) access by index and O(1) amortized pushes, making them the default for ordered sequences and two-pointer scans. When you repeatedly ask 'have I seen this value?' or 'how many times has this appeared?', a Map or Set turns an O(n) search into O(1) average. String problems are usually frequency-map or two-pointer problems in disguise: count characters, compare maps, or sort a canonical key such as a character count signature. The trap is scanning an array inside a loop — if you catch yourself doing that, reach for a map keyed by the value you are searching for.

examples.title: Anagram check with a frequency map
examples.walkthrough: The first pass counts characters in a, the second decrements as it walks b, and any negative count means b used a character a did not have. O(n) time instead of sorting both strings at O(n log n).

content.useCase: Word counts, duplicate detection, two-sum style lookups, anagrams, and caching previously computed values by key.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which structure gives O(1) average membership checks?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Sets and maps hash the value to an index; arrays require scanning to find a value.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why check a.length !== b.length first in the anagram function?
options: Different lengths can never be anagrams, so it exits early
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It is a cheap O(1) rejection that skips unnecessary work.

content.summary: Indexed access means array; lookup by value means map or set. Frequency maps turn most string problems into a single O(n) pass.

lessons.title: Trees and Graph Traversal
objectives: Traverse a tree breadth-first and depth-first
Pick BFS or DFS based on the problem shape

content.introduction: Trees and graphs reduce to two traversal ideas: explore level by level (BFS) or follow one branch to the bottom (DFS). Choosing the right one is often the whole problem.
content.explanation: BFS uses a queue (first in, first out) and visits nodes in order of distance from the root, which makes it the natural tool for shortest paths in unbalanced graphs and for level-by-level output. DFS uses recursion or an explicit stack, needs less memory on shallow trees, and is the default for path, subtree, and backtracking questions. Graphs add one wrinkle: track visited nodes (a Set) or you will loop forever on cyclic structures. Both traversals run in O(V + E) for graphs and O(n) for trees, since every node and edge is processed once.

examples.title: Level-order (BFS) traversal
examples.walkthrough: Capturing queue.length before the inner loop fixes the size of the current level, so each pass collects exactly one level. Children are enqueued after their parent, guaranteeing top-down order.

content.useCase: Level-order printing, shortest path in an unweighted grid, dependency resolution, and 'nearest K nodes' questions.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which traversal visits a tree level by level?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: BFS's queue drains one level before enqueuing the next.

knowledgeCheck.question: What data structure does BFS rely on?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A FIFO queue preserves the order nodes were discovered, which produces level-by-level visits.

content.summary: BFS = queue, level order, shortest path. DFS = stack/recursion, paths and subtrees. Mark visited nodes on graphs.

modules.title: Problem-Solving Strategies
modules.description: Repeatable moves for turning a blank editor into a working, optimized solution.
modules.completionCriteria: Take a fresh problem from clarification to a working optimized solution, stating complexity at each step.

lessons.title: Breaking Down a Problem
objectives: Run a structured clarify-then-plan routine
Move from a brute-force baseline to an optimized solution

content.introduction: Strong candidates do not start typing. They restate the problem, work a small example out loud, state a brute force, then improve it — and the interviewer follows every step.
content.explanation: A reliable sequence is: restate the task in your own words, ask about constraints and edge cases (empty input? duplicates? how large is n?), walk through one concrete example, name the brute-force approach with its complexity, then identify what makes it slow and replace that step. For example, checking every pair for a target sum is O(n^2); the slow step is 'searching the array for the complement', and replacing it with a hash map lookup gives O(n). This narrative shows engineering judgment even if your final code has a bug, which is why interviewers weight it heavily.

examples.title: Brute force upgraded to a hash map
examples.walkthrough: The brute force asks 'does the complement exist?' by scanning; the map answers the same question in O(1). One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space.

content.useCase: The opening two minutes of any coding interview, and the same routine for ambiguous real-world tasks at work.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should happen first when you receive an interview problem?
options: Clarify the problem and work a small example
Start coding the brute force immediately
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Clarifying constraints prevents solving the wrong problem and surfaces edge cases early.

knowledgeCheck.question: In two-sum, which step of the brute force does the hash map replace?
options: Searching the array for the complement value
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The O(n) search becomes an O(1) lookup, which is what drops the whole solution to O(n).

content.summary: Restate, clarify, example, brute force, optimize. Name the slow step before you replace it.

lessons.title: Two Pointers and Sliding Window
objectives: Recognize when a window applies
Implement a window that never backtracks twice

content.introduction: When a problem asks about a contiguous range — longest, shortest, or count of subarrays — a sliding window replaces nested loops with a single pass.
content.explanation: A window is two indices, start and end, that both only move forward. Expand end to include the next element, and shrink start while the window violates a condition (too many distinct characters, sum too large). Because each pointer advances at most n times, the whole scan is O(n) instead of the O(n^2) of enumerating every subarray. Two pointers are the general form: opposite ends for sorted-pair problems (two-sum on a sorted array, container-with-most-water), or both advancing for partition and merge patterns. The key invariant — what is true about the window right now — must be stated out loud before you code it.

examples.title: Longest substring without repeating characters
examples.walkthrough: end always moves forward; when a repeated character appears inside the window, start jumps past its previous position. Each index is visited a constant number of times, so the scan is O(n).

content.useCase: Longest/shortest subarray with a constraint, pair sums in a sorted array, merging sorted lists, and palindromes.

knowledgeCheck.question: When is a sliding window the right tool?
options: The problem involves a contiguous range with a maintainable condition
The input is unsorted and you need a value's index
You must sort the data first
The problem involves a tree only
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Windows work when you can update a summary as elements enter and leave without recomputing.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does the sliding window run in O(n) instead of O(n^2)?
options: Both pointers move only forward, so each element is processed a constant number of times
knowledgeCheck.explanation: There is no backtracking: start and end each advance at most n times.

content.summary: Contiguous range plus a maintainable condition means window. State the invariant, expand end, shrink start.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming Basics
objectives: Spot overlapping subproblems
Convert a memoized recursion into a bottom-up loop

content.introduction: Dynamic programming is just recursion plus remembering. You solve a problem by combining solutions to smaller versions of the same problem — and you never compute the same one twice.
content.explanation: Two properties signal DP: optimal substructure (the best answer combines best answers to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the naive recursion recomputes the same inputs many times). Start with the naive recursive recurrence, add a memo table keyed by the argument to get top-down memoization, then invert it into a bottom-up loop that fills a table or keeps only the values it needs. That last step matters in interviews: Fibonacci as naive recursion is O(2^n), memoized it is O(n), and the iterative form with two rolling variables is O(n) time and O(1) space — no recursion-stack overflow risk.

examples.title: Climbing stairs, bottom-up with O(1) space
examples.walkthrough: Each iteration only needs the previous two values, so the whole table collapses into two variables. Linear time, constant space, and no stack depth to worry about.

content.useCase: Counting paths, edit distance, knapsack-style choices, and any 'min cost to reach the end' grid problem.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which two properties define a dynamic programming problem?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Subproblems must combine into an answer, and they must repeat — otherwise plain recursion suffices.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main benefit of the bottom-up loop over naive recursion?
options: It avoids repeated work and deep call stacks
It removes the need for a base case
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Each state is computed exactly once, and iteration avoids recursion depth limits.

content.summary: Write the recurrence, memoize it, then iterate. Keep only the states the next step actually needs.

modules.title: System Design Foundations
modules.description: Scale a service from one box to many, then design a classic system end to end with stated trade-offs.
modules.completionCriteria: Produce a URL-shortener design that covers requirements, capacity estimates, data storage, and the redirect read path.

lessons.title: Scaling a Web Service
objectives: Explain horizontal scaling and stateless services
Describe the request path through a load-balanced fleet

content.introduction: System design interviews usually start with the same question: this works for 100 users — what breaks at 100,000? The answer is almost always state, single points of failure, and where load lands.
content.explanation: Vertical scaling (bigger machine) hits a ceiling and creates a single point of failure, so systems scale horizontally: add cheap machines behind a load balancer. Horizontal scaling only works if servers are stateless — no session or file state tied to a particular box — because the balancer can send any request to any server. Move session data to a shared store (Redis), uploaded files to object storage, and background jobs to a queue. Then add redundancy at every tier: multiple database replicas, multi-zone deployment, and health checks so the balancer stops routing to dead instances. The classic failure to name in interviews is shared mutable state on the app server.

examples.title: Stateless sessions in Redis
examples.walkthrough: The app server keeps nothing about the user locally. Restart it, replace it, or add five more — every instance reads the same session store, so the load balancer can route freely.

content.useCase: Explaining how a stateless tier plus a load balancer turns one server into a fleet.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why must app servers be stateless to scale horizontally?
options: Any server must be able to handle any request
It removes the need for a database
knowledgeCheck.explanation: If state lives on one box, requests pinned to it break when load balancing moves or removes that box.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which component distributes incoming requests across servers?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The load balancer routes by health and policy, and is the entry point that makes a fleet look like one service.

content.summary: Go horizontal, keep servers stateless, move sessions and files to shared stores, and add redundancy at every tier.

lessons.title: Storage, Indexes, and Caching
objectives: Pick a datastore by access pattern
Implement cache-aside and name its failure mode

content.introduction: Data storage decisions are access-pattern decisions: how you read and write determines whether you want SQL, a document store, a key-value cache, or some combination.
content.explanation: Relational databases give transactions and joins with indexed lookups that keep reads logarithmic — a B-tree index turns a full table scan into ~log n page reads. They struggle when you need huge write throughput or flexible nested documents, which is where key-value and document stores earn their place. Caching sits in front of everything: in cache-aside, the application checks the cache first, loads the database on a miss, and writes the result back with a TTL. The hard part is invalidation — when the row changes, stale cache entries must be evicted or versioned, or users will see old data. Typical interview additions: a read replica to spread SELECT load, and a write-through path so hot rows stay fresh.

examples.title: Cache-aside read path
examples.walkthrough: On a hit the database is never touched. On a miss the app loads the row and stores it for five minutes; the TTL bounds how long stale data can survive if a write is not reflected in the cache.

content.useCase: Read-heavy product catalogs, profile pages, and configuration lookups where a short staleness window is acceptable.

knowledgeCheck.question: In cache-aside, who loads the cache on a miss?
options: The application, after reading the database
The database automatically pushes to the cache
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The app owns the read path: cache first, fall back to the database, then populate the cache.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the classic weakness of caching?
options: Invalidation — keeping cached data consistent with writes
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Stale entries after a write are the hard problem; TTLs, versioned keys, and explicit eviction are the usual mitigations.

content.summary: Match the store to the access pattern, index what you filter on, and use cache-aside with a TTL — knowing invalidation is the real challenge.

lessons.title: Case Study: Design a URL Shortener
objectives: Estimate capacity before designing
Design a read-optimized redirect path

content.introduction: The URL shortener is the interview classic because it forces every core decision: estimate scale, generate unique keys, store mappings, and serve a read path that is almost all traffic.
content.explanation: Start with numbers: 100M new links per day is roughly 1,200 writes/second, and redirects are 100:1 reads, so reads dominate at ~100K/second. Key generation has two realistic options — a hash of the URL (needs collision handling and exposes duplicates) or an auto-incrementing ID encoded in base62 (unique by construction, ~7 characters covers 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion keys). Encode the counter, store id → long_url in SQL with the short code indexed, and put hot mappings in Redis because redirects must return in single-digit milliseconds. The write path is trivial; the design conversation should focus on the read path, analytics counters (asynchronous increments, never inline), and what happens when a link expires.

examples.title: Base62 key encoding
examples.walkthrough: A monotonic ID plus base62 encoding guarantees unique short codes with no lookups. The database's primary key does the uniqueness work you would otherwise pay a retry loop for.

content.useCase: Any 'design X' interview: estimate, generate keys, store, read path, scale the bottleneck.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why prefer an auto-incrementing ID over a random hash for short codes?
options: IDs are unique by construction, so there are no collisions to resolve
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A counter never collides; a hash requires collision detection and retry logic.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should the redirect read be served from in a high-traffic design?
options: A cache like Redis, falling back to the database
A full table scan every time
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Reads massively outnumber writes and redirects are latency-sensitive, so hot mappings belong in the cache.

content.summary: Estimate first, generate keys with a counter, store mappings indexed by short code, and serve the read-heavy path from cache.

modules.title: Behavioral & Communication Skills
modules.description: Structure your answers, narrate your code, and ask the questions that show senior judgment.
modules.completionCriteria: Deliver a two-minute STAR answer and talk through a practice problem end to end without going silent.

lessons.title: The STAR Method for Behavioral Questions
objectives: Structure a behavioral answer in four parts
Quantify the result of your actions

content.introduction: Behavioral questions ('tell me about a time you failed') are scored like system design: structure, specificity, and evidence matter more than the story's drama.
content.explanation: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. Situation sets context in one or two sentences; Task explains what you were personally responsible for; Action is the bulk of the answer — what you specifically did, step by step, using 'I' rather than 'we'; Result closes with a measurable outcome and, ideally, what you learned. Interviewers listen for ownership: a candidate who only describes what the team did has not demonstrated their contribution. Prepare five stories that overlap — a conflict, a failure, a ambiguous requirement, a technical trade-off, a mentoring moment — and map questions onto them. Keep each answer around two minutes and stop; you can always expand if asked.

examples.title: A STAR answer skeleton
examples.walkthrough: Context is one sentence, the action uses concrete steps only you performed, and the result is a number — that is what makes the answer verifiable instead of vague.

content.useCase: Leadership, conflict, failure, and impact questions at any interview stage; also useful in performance reviews.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the T in STAR stand for?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Task states what you were specifically responsible for, between the context and your actions.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which part of a STAR answer should carry measurable outcomes?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Numbers in the Result are what make the claim credible and memorable.

content.summary: Situation, Task, Action, Result — one sentence of context, specific personal actions, quantified outcome.

lessons.title: Talking Through Your Code
objectives: Narrate your approach while you type
Recover gracefully when you get stuck

content.introduction: Silence is the most common avoidable failure in coding interviews. Interviewers score your reasoning in real time, and they can only score what they hear.
content.explanation: A dependable script: restate the problem, state constraints, announce your approach and its complexity, code while narrating each block's intent, then dry-run your solution with a concrete example before declaring it done. When you hit a wall, do not freeze — say what you know ('the two-pointer invariant breaks because the array is unsorted'), try a smaller example, or switch approaches out loud. Ask for clarification whenever a requirement is ambiguous; that is a positive signal. If given a hint, acknowledge it, use it, and explain how it changes your plan — interviewers regularly give hints specifically to see whether you can integrate them.

examples.title: A narrated solution skeleton
examples.walkthrough: Each comment is a beat you say out loud: restate, constraint, approach, code, verify, complexity. The dry run at the end catches off-by-one errors before the interviewer does.

content.useCase: Every coding interview, pairing session, and design review where your thinking is the deliverable.

knowledgeCheck.question: When should you state the complexity of your solution?
options: As part of explaining the approach and again when finished
Only if the interviewer asks nothing else
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Stating complexity up front shows you are choosing between approaches, not just typing.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the best move when you are stuck?
options: Say what you know, try a smaller example, and consider another approach out loud
Sit silently until the answer appears
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Narrating your blocker lets the interviewer help and demonstrates how you debug under uncertainty.

content.summary: Restate, plan, narrate, verify, state complexity. Silence scores zero; a wrong answer with clear reasoning often still scores.

lessons.title: Clarifying Questions and Trade-offs
objectives: Ask questions that reveal requirements
Present options as trade-offs rather than absolutes

content.introduction: The questions you ask are the fastest signal of seniority. Senior candidates turn vague prompts into bounded problems before proposing anything.
content.explanation: For design questions, ask about scale (users, requests per second, data size), consistency needs (is stale data acceptable, and for how long), and failure tolerance (what must keep working when a dependency dies). For coding questions, clarify input constraints, duplicates, and what to return on no match — these decide your algorithm. Then present choices as explicit trade-offs: 'a relational store gives us transactions at the cost of write throughput; a key-value store flips that' is a senior answer, while 'we should use Redis' is not. Also state what you are deliberately not solving — scope boundaries show judgment. Finally, ask one thoughtful question yourself at the end: how the team handles on-call, or how requirements reach engineers.

examples.title: A question checklist to internalize
examples.walkthrough: The questions map to requirements that actually change the architecture; the trade-off statement ties your pick back to those requirements instead of asserting a preference.

content.useCase: Opening any system design interview and closing any technical proposal with a defensible choice.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which question best clarifies a system design requirement?
options: What scale and consistency does this need?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Scale and consistency directly determine the architecture; the others do not.

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes a design choice sound senior?
options: Presenting it as a trade-off tied to stated requirements
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Requirements-based trade-offs show judgment; asserting one 'best' tool ignores context.

content.summary: Clarify scale, consistency, and failure tolerance first. Offer options as trade-offs and name the cost of your choice.
